sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Dumbbell Front Raise is an isolation exercise that targets the anterior (front) deltoid.

Performed standing with dumbbells raised in front of the body to shoulder height, it is a staple movement for building shoulder definition and strength.

This exercise is commonly used in shoulder training routines to develop the front portion of the deltoid muscle.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Directly isolates the anterior deltoid
- Builds shoulder definition and roundness from the front
- Strengthens the shoulder for pressing movements
- Simple to learn with minimal equipment required
- Can be performed unilaterally to correct imbalances
- Improves shoulder stability and endurance
- Effective at lighter weights with strict form

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Anterior Deltoid

Secondary: Lateral Deltoid, Upper Chest (Clavicular Head of Pectoralis Major), Trapezius, Serratus Anterior, Core (stabilisation)

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand upright with feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing your thighs (pronated grip).
3. Let the dumbbells rest against the front of your thighs.
4. Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout the movement.
5. Engage your core and maintain a neutral spine.
6. Pull your shoulders back and down, away from your ears.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Keeping your arms straight with a slight bend in the elbows, raise the dumbbells in front of your body.
2. Exhale as you lift the dumbbells to shoulder height — arms parallel to the floor.
3. Pause briefly at the top of the movement and squeeze the front deltoids.
4. Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position while inhaling.
5. Maintain control throughout the entire range of motion.
6. Repeat for the desired number of reps.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Swinging the dumbbells or using momentum to lift
- Raising the dumbbells above shoulder height unnecessarily
- Shrugging the shoulders up during the lift
- Arching the lower back to compensate for heavy weight
- Fully locking out the elbows
- Rushing the lowering phase
- Using too heavy a weight, sacrificing strict form

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Pair of Dumbbells (appropriate weight for controlled reps)
- Open floor space for standing
- Optional: Mirror for form checking

sections.heading: Selecting Your Weight
sections.content:
1. The front raise is an isolation movement — start light.
2. Choose a weight you can lift with strict form for 10-15 reps.
3. You should be able to pause at the top without swinging.
4. If your lower back arches or you need momentum, reduce the weight.
5. Progress gradually, prioritising time under tension over load.
6. This is a high-rep, controlled movement — ego lifting is counterproductive.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Shoulder-width apart, flat on the floor.
2. Knees: Slight bend, not locked.
3. Hips: Neutral position, core braced.
4. Torso: Upright, shoulders back and down.
5. Arms: Slight bend in elbows, dumbbells resting on thighs.
6. Grip: Overhand (pronated), palms facing the body.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes forward.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Arnold Press: Rotational press that heavily involves the anterior deltoid
- Barbell Overhead Press: Compound pressing for overall shoulder development
- Cable Front Raise: Constant tension variation using cables
- Plate Front Raise: Alternative using a weight plate
- Lateral Raise: Targets the lateral (side) deltoid
- Dumbbell Shoulder Press: Compound movement for all three deltoid heads

sections.heading: Front Raise Variations
sections.content:
Alternating Front Raise: Raise one arm at a time for unilateral focus
Seated Front Raise: Performed seated to eliminate lower body momentum
Incline Front Raise: Lying face down on an incline bench for a stretch
Neutral Grip Front Raise: Palms facing each other (hammer grip)
Barbell Front Raise: Both arms using a barbell for bilateral loading
Cable Front Raise: Using a low cable for constant tension

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Pain: Reduce the range of motion or use a neutral grip
Lower Back Issues: Perform seated or brace against a wall
Wrist Discomfort: Use a neutral (hammer) grip variation
No Dumbbells: Use resistance bands, cables, or a weight plate
Mobility Restrictions: Start with partial range of motion and progress over time
Recovering from Injury: Use very light weight and focus on controlled movement
